name: Illusion of validity
statement: Confidence in a prediction tracks how neatly the evidence fits a story, not how well it predicts, so consistent and redundant inputs produce the most assured judgements.
meaning: The claim separates two things that feel like one. How sure a forecaster should be depends on how much the evidence can tell him, which is a property of its validity. How sure he is depends on how well the evidence composes into a picture of the outcome, which is a property of the fit. Those come apart most sharply when inputs are redundant. Several correlated scores say close to what one score says, and they say it without contradicting each other, so the picture is clean while the information added is small. Tversky and Kahneman put the consequence plainly in their 1973 technical report: because redundancy usually raises confidence and lowers accuracy, people have most confidence in the predictions most likely to be off the mark. The illusion is named for its persistence. Their account holds that it survives the judge knowing the record of judges like him.

origin.note: The term entered print in "On the psychology of prediction", 80(4), 237-251, where it names a section on why fit drives confidence. Kahneman says he coined it years earlier, as a lieutenant in the Israel Defence Forces psychology branch, and that it reached the technical literature almost twenty years later. The same argument appears as point five of Tversky and Kahneman's review "Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases", issued in August 1973 as an Oregon Research Institute report for the Office of Naval Research and published in Science the following year.

evidence: The founding paper's own demonstration is its Study 6, and it measures confidence alone. Each of 130 participants saw one student's scores on a pair of aptitude tests described as correlated with each other, and another student's scores on a pair described as uncorrelated. They predicted a grade point average for each and rated how sure they were. Confidence was higher for the correlated pair, t(129) = 4.80, p < .001. There is no accuracy criterion in that design, because the students are hypothetical and no true grade exists. The 1973 report states the mechanism in general form: given inputs of stated validity, a prediction from independent inputs can beat a prediction from redundant ones, while redundancy is what makes a profile look internally consistent and so makes it feel diagnostic. The report also names the applied case, arguing that selection interviewers keep their confidence despite a literature showing the interview to be fallible. Kahneman's own account of that case is autobiographical. Assessing officer candidates for the Israeli army in the mid-1950s, he watched groups of eight men, insignia removed, carry a telephone pole over a 2.5-metre wall without touching either. He and a colleague felt they could see who would lead. Monthly feedback from the officer-training school put the accuracy of those ratings at negligible, and the next day's candidates produced the same sense of insight. He also reports that a structured interview schedule he then designed raised validity, with correlations of close to .30 against about .10 for the previous method, and he gives both as recollection. The nearest thing to a systematic accuracy record is the clinical-versus-mechanical literature. Grove and colleagues meta-analysed 136 studies of health and behaviour in which a judge and a formula worked from the same predictors, with a weighted mean effect of 0.086 on their transformed scale, SD 0.12, median 0.080. Under their rubric, 63 studies of the 136 favoured the formula by a pragmatic margin, 65 were level, and 8 favoured the clinician. The variable that mattered most is the one the illusion predicts: where a clinical interview was among the predictors the mean effect against the judge was 0.224, against 0.070 where it was not, t(134) = 5.02, p < .0001. Ægisdóttir and colleagues, reviewing 56 years of mental-health prediction, report in their abstract 67 studies and 92 effect sizes, with a 13% accuracy gain for statistical methods in their most stringent subset. The dissociation has also been produced directly. Hall, Ariss and Todorov had participants predict National Basketball Association games from win records and half-time scores, with half also given the team names. Names left accuracy flat or lowered it while raising the confidence of fans, who in one experiment reached 6.29 on a nine-point scale against 5.23 without names. In a betting version with 20 participants and outcome feedback after every game, those given names earned $1.64 against $2.78, t(19) = 2.35, p < .03, and most still believed the names had helped. Outside the laboratory, Ben-David, Graham and Harvey collected more than 13,300 market-return distributions from company executives over ten years and found realised returns inside the executives' own 80% intervals 36% of the time.

replication.headline: The confidence half of the effect repeated cleanly in a preregistered sample four times the original size, and nobody has replicated the accuracy half because the original never measured it.
replication.detail: Chan and Feldman registered a replication of all seven studies in Kahneman and Tversky (1973), and Peer Community in Registered Reports granted it in-principle acceptance in May 2024. Study 6, the illusion-of-validity demonstration, came out as the original did. With 397 US participants on Prolific, confidence was higher predicting from correlated inputs, 62.47 against 55.99 on a 0 to 100 scale, t(396) = 8.30, p < .001, d = 0.42, 95% CI [0.31, 0.52]. A control group of 394, who saw the same two test pairs with the correlated and uncorrelated labels swapped, gave 66.57 against 56.42, d = 0.63, 95% CI [0.52, 0.74]. The switch rules out the test contents driving the result. What the replication cannot do is show the confidence was misplaced, since the original design has no correct answer to score against. The report is candid that higher confidence is not by itself evidence that people were judging by representativeness. Its overall verdict on the 1973 paper is mixed rather than clean. The same sample reversed the paper's Study 7 on regression: where 73 of 108 of the original respondents gave an interval symmetric around the observed score, 17.60% of the replication sample did and 76.40% gave a regressive one.

study.cite: Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Bachelor of Social Sciences thesis, University of Hong Kong, with results, materials and data deposited at OSF project 8zhcj.

limits: The 1973 paper itself could not be opened. Unpaywall records it as closed with no repository copy, OpenAlex lists no open location, PsycNet served no text, Semantic Scholar holds no record under its DOI, and the two CiteSeerX links OpenAlex carries did not resolve. So its Study 6 design, its sample of 130 and its t(129) = 4.80 are read from the tables of the replication report rather than from the original, and the abstract quoted from it is the published abstract as carried by OpenAlex. The passage that gives the term its meaning is quoted here at one remove too, from Einhorn and Hogarth's verbatim quotation of page 249. Tversky and Kahneman's general statement of the redundancy argument was read in full, in the scanned Oregon Research Institute report rather than in Science. The replication is a Stage 1 registered report whose results exist as an undergraduate thesis deposited on OSF; no peer-reviewed Stage 2 was located in Crossref, in the OSF project, at Peer Community in Registered Reports, or by open-web search, and the project's files had not changed since May 2024. That thesis contradicts itself once, giving df = 396 in its text and 399 in its summary table for the same test. No effect size is printed for the original, because neither the replication nor any other source consulted supplies one, and computing one here from t and n would be arithmetic rather than reading. Kahneman's army figures cannot be checked: the .30 and .10 correlations are his own recollection in a memoir written decades later, and no data from the unit was published. Ægisdóttir and colleagues stayed behind a paywall, and their two figures come from the published abstract at ERIC. Törngren and Montgomery's study of stock-market professionals, the closest match to the question of analysts' confidence against their accuracy, was closed at the publisher, closed at Semantic Scholar and blocked at ResearchGate, so nothing from it appears above.
misreadings: The story everyone tells about the illusion of validity is the officer-selection story, and it is not the evidence for it. Kahneman coined the phrase there and published no data from it; the correlations he quotes are remembered, and the experiment that carries the name is a grade-prediction task run on students. The second error runs the other way. Study 6 shows that consistent inputs raise confidence, and shows nothing about whether they lower accuracy, because the predicted students do not exist. Treating the replication as proof that confident forecasters are wrong reads a result out of a design that could not produce it. The clinical-versus-mechanical literature is also flattened in the retelling. Grove and colleagues did not find that judges are useless: half of their 136 studies were level and 8 favoured the clinician, and the finding with teeth is narrower, that the gap widens when an interview is one of the predictors. Finally, the illusion is not the same as general overconfidence. It is a claim about which predictions attract the most confidence, and its prediction is specific: the redundant, tidy, story-shaped case, rather than the ambiguous one.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1973). On the psychology of prediction. Psychological Review, 80(4), 237-251. Closed access on every route tried; the bibliographic record was verified at Crossref and the published abstract read through OpenAlex. No figure attributed to this paper above was read in it.

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1973). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. ONR Technical Report, Oregon Research Institute, August 1973, AD-767 426. Read in full as the scanned report at the Internet Archive; the source for the section on the illusion of validity and the redundancy argument.

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. The journal version of the report above, cited so a reader can find it; the text quoted here is the report's.

Kahneman, D. (2003). Autobiography. In T. Frangsmyr (Ed.), Les Prix Nobel 2002. Read in full at nobelprize.org. The source for the officer-selection account, the coinage of the term, and the remembered validity figures.

Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973). University of Hong Kong thesis, deposited at OSF. Read in full; the source for every replication figure above, including the original study's t value.

Rahal, R.-M. (2024). The Representativeness Heuristic Revisited: Registered Replication Report of Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Peer Community in Registered Reports. The Stage 1 in-principle acceptance of the replication above, dated 31 May 2024.

Grove, W. M., Zald, D. H., Lebow, B. S., Snitz, B. E., & Nelson, C. (2000). Clinical versus mechanical prediction: A meta-analysis. Psychological Assessment, 12(1), 19-30. Read in full; the source for the 136 studies, the weighted mean and the interview comparison.

Ægisdóttir, S., White, M. J., Spengler, P. M., Maugherman, A. S., Anderson, L. A., Cook, R. S., Nichols, C. N., Lampropoulos, G. K., Walker, B. S., Cohen, G., & Rush, J. D. (2006). The Meta-Analysis of Clinical Judgment Project: Fifty-six years of accumulated research on clinical versus statistical prediction. The Counseling Psychologist, 34(3), 341-382. Closed access; the study count and the 13% figure are read from the published abstract at ERIC, record EJ735126.

Hall, C. C., Ariss, L., & Todorov, A. (2007). The illusion of knowledge: When more information reduces accuracy and increases confidence. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 103(2), 277-290. Read in full; the source for the basketball accuracy, confidence and earnings figures.

Ben-David, I., Graham, J. R., & Harvey, C. R. (2013). Managerial miscalibration. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(4), 1547-1584. Read in full from the author copy at Duke; the source for the 36% coverage of executives' 80% intervals.

Einhorn, H. J., & Hogarth, R. M. (1978). Confidence in judgment: Persistence of the illusion of validity. Psychological Review, 85(5), 395-416. Read in full. It quotes page 249 of the 1973 paper verbatim, and models why outcome feedback on accepted cases sustains confidence rather than correcting it.

Kahneman, D., & Klein, G. (2009). Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree. American Psychologist, 64(6), 515-526. Read in full; the source for Kahneman's later gloss on the illusion as overconfidence in low-validity environments.
